units.label: 预训练MLM偏好基准及race分布分析
units.description: 四模型在CPS/SS共享IME及比较指标；race Welch和ECDF为同批输出的辅助分析。

units.label: CPS人工标签一致性
units.description: 复用CPS标注，以ROC/AUROC检验U001各句分数与有偏/无偏标签关系。

units.label: 定向MLMO重训练及前后偏差比较
units.description: 每基座分别以Sdis/Sadv训练，BSRT及McNemar比较；训练过程服务本比较。

units.label: 重训练方向一致性验证
units.description: 复用U003分数，以两训练方向的预期标签计算72格预测的方向错误。

facts.statement: 研究以MLMO下成对句子的ground-truth token预测质量代理MLM对刻板/反刻板句子的相对偏好，比较预训练偏差、人工标注一致性及重训练引入的变化；不是去偏算法。

method_function.text: 界定偏差构念及验证范围

facts.statement: 四个模型bert-base-uncased、roberta-base、distilbert-base-uncased、distilroberta-base共用评分流程。U001预训练基准；U002人工标注验证为其辅助分析；U003重训练比较；U004是U003的方向一致性验证，重复使用同批分数，不是72个独立训练实验。

method_function.text: 区分共享模型条件与分析层级

facts.statement: CPS使用九类全部成对句子，Sdis为对弱势群体有偏刻板句，Sadv为对优势群体有偏反刻板句；SS仅用intrasentence四类，排除intersentence。表5 CPS每组1508句，类别race516/religion105/nationality159/socioeconomic172/gender262/sexual orientation84/age87/disability60/appearance63；SS每组2106句（962/79/255/810）。

method_function.text: 确定配对材料和类别分母

facts.statement: IME逐一遮盖原句token，n个token获得n次预测；每次上下文含除ground-truth外全部token，非逐步用预测词替换原句。排除特殊首尾token。

method_function.text: 固定上下文并逐token探测

facts.statement: 取概率最高/排名第一的预测token tp及真实masked token tm；CRR(w)=1−1/rank(tm)，修改后ΔP(w)=log P(tp|c)−log P(tm|c)。越接近0解释为越偏好该原句。

method_function.text: 把预测质量转为token代理分数

facts.statement: 注意力aw为真实token关联的multi-head attentions平均。印刷式4为CRRA(w)=aw[1−log(ρ(tm|c)^−1)]，式5为ΔPA(w)=aw[log P(tp|c)−log P(tm|c)]。CRR、ΔP、CRRA、ΔPA句级分数均以ls为分母平均token分数；未给attention层/方向的进一步选取规则。

method_function.text: 注意力加权及句级聚合

facts.statement: 复现对照为CSPS、SSS、AUL、AULA：CSPS以修改token为上下文，对未修改token的逐token掩码log概率求和；SSS由未修改上下文预测修改token、印刷式12仍写1/lsΣt∈s；AUL为完整不遮盖原句各token log概率平均，AULA再乘attention。CSPS只用于CPS，SSS只用于SS。

method_function.text: 保留比较器操作而非只列名称

facts.statement: 先对每对i算ΔfT(i)：M1={CRR,CRRA,ΔP,ΔPA}用f(Sadv)−f(Sdis)，M2={AUL,AULA,CSPS,SSS}反向；BSPT=100/NΣI(ΔfT(i)>0)，N为当前类别/总体的句对数，等于0计0，>50解释为更偏向对弱势群体有偏句。

method_function.text: 统一指标方向并计算预训练比例

facts.statement: BSRT=100/NΣI(ΔfT1(i)>ΔfT2(i))，T1为重训练、T2同类预训练基座；>50解释为重训练增加对Sdis的相对偏好，<50反之。这不是简单BSPT相减，也不是偏差幅度均值。

method_function.text: 成对比较模型前后的偏好变化

facts.statement: 对各指标及同模型两个句组间的差做Shapiro–Wilk正态性检验；作者报告未发现非正态证据。

method_function.text: 检查指标分布假设

facts.statement: 复用CPS每对5名标注者加作者隐含标注：至少3/6认为socially biased且认为有偏者对类型多数一致才标有偏，得到1450有偏/58无偏对。计算每句指标、变化阈值作binary分类和ROC/AUROC；文字称分别为Sdis/Sadv阈值最大化AUC，未给可执行阈值选择及句到对合并规则。

method_function.text: 以已有人工标签检验评分一致性

facts.statement: 图4/5显示RoBERTa与BERT人工标签AUC约0.53–0.57。正文报告至少一个提出指标优于AUL/AULA；图中并非所有提出指标均更好，不能宣称高效度或普遍优胜。

method_function.text: 限定一致性结果

facts.statement: 各模型分别在CPS Sdis或Sadv重训练MLMO；RoBERTa系列用cased、BERT系列uncased，PyTorch、P100/T4；mlm_probability=.15、训练80%/验证20%、30 epochs，作者报epoch30最低验证loss。每组1508行、>1.9×10^4 tokens，表6给cased/uncased词汇量与lexical diversity。

method_function.text: 有意改变训练语料偏向建立方向检验

facts.statement: 用CRR句分数画Sdis与Sadv的ECDF差，race/RoBERTa图1显示Sdis重训练上移、Sadv重训练下移；附录J给预训练四模型图。

method_function.text: 分布层面对偏好变化作图

facts.statement: 前后模型按fR(Sadv)>fR(Sdis)、fP(Sadv)>fP(Sdis)二值结果配成列联表，用McNemar边际同质性检验p<.05；表15–18用†标显著，未显著格不着色。

method_function.text: 检验配对二值偏差比例变化

facts.statement: ΔP/ΔPA在各模型两训练方向和九类别均报告显著比例变化；CRRA在distilBERT/Sdis/disability的BSRT为46.67，说明有未符合预期方向个案。作者据较极端分数及较多显著结果解释其更敏感。

method_function.text: 保留主要方向与反例

facts.statement: 方向验证把BSRT>50映为1、<50为0，Sdis重训练预期1、Sadv预期0；每指标4模型×2方向×9类=72个预测，一半各类真值。按是否符合训练方向算错误率；==50处理未写。

method_function.text: 按训练方向预期检验指标

facts.statement: 正文报CRR/ΔP/ΔPA准确率100%、CRRA99%、AUL93%、AULA88%、CSPS94%；表4按模型/训练方向列0.028/0.083等错误率，其分母与九类单格不吻合，不能据该表无歧义重建正文总体准确率。

method_function.text: 披露汇总口径冲突

facts.statement: 附录K.0.1和表19另对race两句组各提出指标做双尾Welch t检验p<.05，报告mean f(Sadv)−mean f(Sdis)，按数据集各组N等长；不是成对t检验。

method_function.text: 补充比较race句分数分布

facts.statement: 整体BSPT与分类别结果因模型、数据集和指标而不同；表2 BERT的AUL/AULA在CPS低于50，其余提出指标多高于50。不能将不同指标的偏差排序等同。

method_function.text: 限定模型偏差结论对测量方式的依赖

facts.statement: 作者将范围限于英语、二元句组、已有类别与人工标签、四类MLM及MLMO；未来讨论不同目标/架构/训练语料、重训练条件与语料偏差一致性，不视作已实施验证。

method_function.text: 保留泛化边界与未来建议

To address the issue of social biases in MLMs
at its source, we measure biases of MLMs while
focusing on an MLM’s key pretraining objective:
masked language modeling. In this work, we focus
on proposing and assessing bias evaluation measures for MLMs and not proposing methods for
debiasing MLMs. However, when assessing evaluation measures, we consider prior research that
involves retraining or fine-tuning under the MLMO
with debiased or counterfactual data to reduce biases in MLMs, such as Zhao et al., 2018 and Zhao
et al., 2019 which use data augmentation to swap
gendered words with their opposites prior to retraining. Motivated by this, we assess whether proposed measures satisfy an important criterion for
improvement over previously proposed ones: align-

We denote pre- and retrained transformers as
TP and TR respectively. The subscript unc denotes an uncased model. We report results from
the following transformer-based language models
available through the HuggingFace library (Wolf
et al., 2020): bert-base-uncased (BERTunc ; Devlin
et al., 2019), roberta-base (RoBERTa; Liu et al.,
2019b), distilbert-base-uncased (distilBERTunc ;
Sanh et al., 2019), and distilroberta-base (distilRoBERTa; Liu et al., 2019a).

for four forms of social biases, using the likelihood of modified tokens given unmodified token
contexts as proxy for MLM preference. Similarly,
CPS contains characteristic words that distinguish
sentences within pairs and define the nature of a
particular bias towards either advantaged or disadvantaged groups, but instead uses the relative
likelihood of unmodified tokens being chosen by
the MLM given a modified context (characteristic
word) across a sentence pair.
CPS and SS contain biased sentences towards
advantaged and disadvantaged groups, where CPS
sentence pairs are categorized by bias types: race,
age, socioeconomic, disability, religion, physical
appearance, gender, sexual orientation, and nationality, and SS sentence pairs by: race, religion, gender, and profession (see Appendix A.1 for details
on sentence counts for bias categories).
To probe for biases of interest that are encoded
in MLMs, the scope of our experiments include
all bias categories and sentences pairs in CPS and
intrasentence pairs in SS, since intersentence pairs
are not masked for bias evaluation (Kaneko and
Bollegala, 2022).11 We estimate MLM preference
towards a stereotypical sentence over a less stereotypical one for each bias category in CPS and SS.

4.4.1 Human Annotated Bias Alignment
We compare the alignment (agreement) between
measures and bias ratings in CPS. Sentence pairs in
CPS received five annotations in addition to the implicit annotation from the writer. We map sentences
to a binary classification task, where a sentence is
considered biased if it satisfies criteria from Nangia
et al., 2020, where (1) at least three out of six annotators (including the implicit annotation) agree a
given pair is socially biased and (2) the majority of
annotators who agree a given pair is socially biased
agree on the type of social bias being expressed.14
We compute evaluation measures derived from
MLMs to predict whether a pair is biased or unbiased at varying thresholds. All measures are
computed for each sentence in a pair. Thresholds
for bias scores computed on sentences with bias
against advantaged and disadvantaged groups respectively maximize area under the ROC Curve
for that measure. We find that one or more of proposed measures ∆PA and CRRA, along with modified ∆P and CRR, outperform AUL and AULA in
their agreement with human annotators on CPS for

4.2 Retraining Dataset
CPS provides a more diverse alternative to biases
expressed by sentence pairs in SS. Biases widely
acknowledged in the United States are well represented in CPS12 compared to SS, and there is
greater diversity of sentence structures in CPS
(Nangia et al., 2020). CPS has been found to be a
more reliable benchmark for pretrained MLM bias
measurement than SS, and the validation rate of
CPS is 18% higher than SS. (Nangia et al., 2020).
Based on these findings, paired with (1) the computational expense and time-consumption involved
with retraining MLMs under the MLMO and (2)
concerns regarding standard masked language modeling metric viability on SS, we proceed to use sentence sets in CPS to re-train MLMs and validate
methods for estimating the biases that are introduced (Nangia et al., 2020) (see Appendix A.2 for
details). We re-train MLMs ∀s ∈ Sdis or ∀s ∈ Sadv ,

We re-train each transformer under consideration
using the PyTorch Python library with P100 and T4
GPUs on cased (RoBERTa and distilRoBERTa) and
uncased (BERTunc and distilBERTunc ) versions of
CPS sentences (see Appendix M.1 for more details).

M.1 Experiment Settings
We retrain MLMs with mlm_probability set to
0.15 (as in Devlin et al., 2019), using 80 percent
of data for training and 20 percent for validation.
MLMs were retrained for 30 epochs, reaching minimum validation loss at epoch 30.

4.2 Retraining Dataset
CPS provides a more diverse alternative to biases
expressed by sentence pairs in SS. Biases widely
acknowledged in the United States are well represented in CPS12 compared to SS, and there is
greater diversity of sentence structures in CPS
(Nangia et al., 2020). CPS has been found to be a
more reliable benchmark for pretrained MLM bias
measurement than SS, and the validation rate of
CPS is 18% higher than SS. (Nangia et al., 2020).
Based on these findings, paired with (1) the computational expense and time-consumption involved
with retraining MLMs under the MLMO and (2)
concerns regarding standard masked language modeling metric viability on SS, we proceed to use sentence sets in CPS to re-train MLMs and validate
methods for estimating the biases that are introduced (Nangia et al., 2020) (see Appendix A.2 for
details). We re-train MLMs ∀s ∈ Sdis or ∀s ∈ Sadv ,

and distilBERTunc according to (1) all but one measure on SS and (2) AUL and CRRA on CPS.

Limitations

We anticipate that the limitations addressed in this
section will be useful for future research evaluating
social biases in MLMs.
As described in section 4, we leverage sentence
pairs from two benchmark datasets, CPS and SS,
to evaluate the social biases of pre- and retrained
MLMs. Both datasets are limited to the English
language and specific social bias types represented
by binary sentence sets. Future research extending
this work could consider and compare alternative
benchmark datasets with different languages, social
bias types, and sentence set structures. In addition,

we acknowledge the dependency on human annotated biases in benchmark datasets when assessing
discussed measures.
In this work, and as mentioned in section 2.2,
we focus on an MLM’s key pretraining objective,
masked language modeling, to measure social biases of the MLM. Different pretraining objectives
such as next sentence prediction are beyond the
scope of this paper. Furthermore, we measure relative changes in biases w.r.t. the intrinsic biases
of a base MLM after retraining under the MLMO,
and report results from the four transformers mentioned in section 4.3. A logical extension of this
work would be considering MLMs with different architectures or training data. We propose the modelcomparative function BSRT to measure the relative
change in MLM biases after retraining. Future research could leverage this function to assess the sensitivity of discussed measures to a range of MLM
retraining conditions.
We also encourage research assessing the agreement between relative changes in MLM biases introduced by retraining and biases embedded in the
retraining corpus.

7

Ethical Considerations

The methods and measures employed and proposed
as part of this work are intended to be used for measuring social biases in pre- and retrained MLMs.
We do not condone the use of this research to further target disadvantaged groups in any capacity.
Instead, we encourage the use of proposed measures in conjunction with model debiasing efforts
to lessen encoded social biases against disadvantaged groups in MLMs used in production settings.
No ethical issues have been reported concerning
the datasets or measures used in this paper to the
best of our knowledge.
